questions.q: What was the exact compromise formula proposed by the Language Committee of the Constituent Assembly in 1949 regarding the official language of the Union?
questions.a: The Language Committee recommended: (1) Hindi in Devanagari script shall be the official language of the Union; (2) English shall continue for all official purposes for 15 years from the commencement of the Constitution; (3) Parliament may by law provide for continued use of English after 15 years; (4) Each province may choose one regional language for official work within the province. A wrong answer (e.g., “Hindi was made the national language”) reveals confusion between *official language* (Article 343) and *national language* (a term the Constitution deliberately avoids), and misses the 15-year transitional guarantee for English.

questions.q: Why did Mahatma Gandhi insist on Hindustani (a blend of Hindi and Urdu) rather than Sanskritised Hindi as the national language, and how did Partition alter the political feasibility of his position?
questions.a: Gandhi saw Hindustani as a composite, spoken language of the masses that bridged Hindu-Muslim and North-South divides; he called confining oneself to Hindi or Urdu “a crime against intelligence and patriotism” (Harijan Sevak, 12 Oct 1947). Partition and the departure of Muslim League members removed the Urdu-speaking constituency from the Assembly, while communal violence empowered advocates of Sanskritised Hindi who equated Hindi with Hindu identity. A wrong answer that says “Gandhi wanted Hindi” misses the critical distinction between *Hindustani* (pluralistic, Persian-Arabic inclusive) and *Hindi* (Sanskritised, exclusionary), and fails to link Partition to the shift in Assembly arithmetic.

questions.q: A member from Madras tells the Assembly in 1949: “We accepted Hindustani on Gandhi’s call, started schools, braved resistance. Now that language is being changed — Urdu words removed, Sanskrit words added. This propaganda for Hindi cuts at the root of provincial languages.” Using this source, explain *why* non-Hindi speakers felt betrayed rather than merely inconvenienced.
questions.a: The speaker (G. Durgabai) highlights a broken *political contract*: the Congress had mobilised southern volunteers for Hindustani as a *composite* national language; the unilateral Sanskritisation after Gandhi’s death and Partition turned that contract into imposition. The betrayal is political — the inclusive symbol they worked for was replaced by an exclusionary one — not merely linguistic. A wrong answer focusing only on “difficulty in learning Hindi” misses the *breach of trust* and the *symbolic violence* of redefining the national language after minorities had invested in the earlier vision.

questions.q: Compare R.V. Dhulekar’s 1949 demand (“Hindi must be the *national* language, not merely official”) with the Language Committee’s compromise. Identify *two* specific constitutional mechanisms the compromise introduced to prevent Dhulekar’s majoritarian vision from becoming permanent.
questions.a: (1) Article 343’s 15-year English continuation clause (extendable by Parliament) — a *sunset clause* on Hindi’s exclusivity. (2) The Eighth Schedule (Articles 344, 351) listing 14 languages — an *institutionalised pluralism* that obliges the Union to develop *all* scheduled languages, not just Hindi. A wrong answer listing only “English continued for 15 years” misses the *positive obligation* on the Centre to promote scheduled languages (Article 351), which structurally prevents Hindi from crowding out others.

questions.q: Evaluate the historian Granville Austin’s judgement that the language compromise was “a masterpiece of constructive ambiguity.” Support your evaluation with *two* specific provisions that created flexibility and *one* provision that created rigidity.
questions.a: Flexibility: (a) Article 343(2)–(3) — Parliament can extend English indefinitely; (b) Article 351 — Directive to develop Hindi *by assimilating* forms from scheduled languages, making Hindi’s evolution open-ended. Rigidity: Article 343(1) — Hindi in Devanagari *shall* be the official language (no “may”), fixing the script and base language permanently. A wrong answer calling the whole thing “flexible” ignores the mandatory Devanagari/Hindi anchor; one calling it “rigid” ignores the extendable English window and the developmental mandate for other languages.

questions.q: Construct a 5-event timeline (1946–1950) showing how the language question moved from *consensus on Hindustani* to *compromise on Official Hindi + Eighth Schedule*. For each event, name the key actor or body and the decisive shift.
questions.a: 1. Dec 1946 – Nehru’s Objectives Resolution: “adequate safeguards for minorities” (framework). 2. 1947 – Gandhi’s last Hindustani statement (Harijan Sevak): composite language ideal. 3. Aug 1947 – Partition: Muslim League exits, Urdu constituency gone. 4. Sept 1949 – Language Committee (Munshi-Ayyangar) Report: Official Hindi + 15-year English + Eighth Schedule. 5. Jan 1950 – Constitution adopted: Articles 343–351 encode compromise. A poor timeline omits Partition as the *turning point* or treats the Language Committee report as the start rather than the *resolution* of three years of deadlock.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Language Debate in the ______ Assembly (1946–1949) was a prolonged and contentious discussion on whether Hindi, Hindustani, or English should serve as the official/national language of the Indian Union, culminating in the Munshi-Ayyangar compromise: Hindi in Devanagari as the official language of the Union with English continuing for 15 years, and the Eighth Schedule listing initially 14 regional languages for development.
Fill in the blank: Imagine holding a ₹200 banknote — you see Hindi and English on the front, and 15 other ______ on the reverse.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Can explain the three main positions (Hindi, Hindustani, English) with their political backers, trace the evolution from Gandhi’s Hindustani to the Sanskritised Hindi push, analyze the Munshi-Ayyangar compromise formula, and evaluate how the Eighth Schedule institutionalised linguistic pluralism rather than imposing monolingual unity.
